system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-11-24 21:19:00 to 2185-11-26 13:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a history of chronic diastolic heart failure, alcoholic cirrhosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and prior right knee replacement presented with increasing right knee pain and systemic symptoms after completing a course of IV antibiotics for a prosthetic joint infection. She was found to have elevated inflammatory markers and was admitted for surgical intervention. She underwent removal of an infected antibiotic spacer, irrigation and debridement, and placement of a new antibiotic-loaded spacer. The postoperative course was stable, with resolution of fever and good wound healing. IV antibiotics were discontinued due to negative cultures, and she was transitioned to oral pain control. She was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with instructions for anticoagulation, wound care, and activity restrictions.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to internal joint prosthesis
Surgical operation with implant of artificial internal device causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication,without mention of misadventure at time of operation
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I had a really bad episode a few days ago—my toilet was filled with bright red blood after a bowel movement. My PCP called me when my blood count came back low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds scary. Since then, have you had any more bloody stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since that one time. But I’ve had a lot of watery brown diarrhea. No more blood, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned you have Crohn’s disease. Has it been active lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. My last colonoscopy didn’t show active Crohn’s—just hemorrhoids. But I’ve had some crampy pain in my upper belly since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that. We gave you Tylenol, but it hasn’t helped much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, the pain is still there, but it’s not getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your hemoglobin was quite low—7.3 when you arrived. That’s why we’re giving you blood transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember getting one unit earlier today. How many will I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get three units total. Your body needs time to recover from the blood loss. We’re watching you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the bleeding still going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No active bleeding now. The colonoscopy showed internal hemorrhoids and some diverticula, which are likely the source. No signs of Crohn’s flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not my Crohn’s. But I’m worried—my mom died of colon cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your colon looked normal aside from the hemorrhoids and diverticula. No tumors or concerning lesions were seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other stomach pain? The EGD showed ulcers, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there were ulcers and erosions in your stomach. That could be contributing to your pain. We’ve started you on a medication called pantoprazole to help heal them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also on mesalamine for Crohn’s. Should I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it. Since there’s no active inflammation, it’s safe. But we’ve made a few other medication changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your clopidogrel—also called Plavix—because of the recent bleeding. And we lowered your aspirin dose to 81 mg. You’ll need to talk to your cardiologist about restarting them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I was on those for my heart. I hope it’s okay to stop them temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s the right move for now. Your safety comes first. We’ll balance heart and GI risks with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your second blood transfusion went well overnight. Your latest hemoglobin is up to 10.8, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. My stomach pain is also better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. No more diarrhea or blood in your stool either. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’s wonderful. Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll need to see your PCP and GI doctor soon. We’ll also send a note to your cardiologist about the medication changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my knee pain? I’ve been using oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue the oxycodone for now, but avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can irritate your stomach and increase bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll stick to Tylenol and oxycodone as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, please follow a low-sodium diet—no more than 2 grams per day—and weigh yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any other warnings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Return to the ER if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, bloody stools, fevers, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home. Your labs are stable, and you’ve had no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your medications: pantoprazole daily, aspirin at 81 mg, and clopidogrel held. Please follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make those calls. And I’ll watch my diet and weight like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, diastolic heart failure, alcoholic cirrhosis, and recent gastrointestinal bleeding presented with a single episode of bright red blood per rectum and a significantly low hemoglobin. She was admitted for management of acute posthemorrhagic anemia and received three units of packed red blood cells. Evaluation revealed internal hemorrhoids and diverticulosis as the likely source of bleeding, with no active Crohn’s disease. An EGD showed gastric ulcers, and she was started on pantoprazole. Clopidogrel was held and aspirin dose reduced due to bleeding risk. Her condition stabilized, hemoglobin improved, and she was discharged home in good condition with follow-up plans and medication adjustments.
